## **Notes** 

#### Units used: 

Unless otherwise stated, all statistics on platinum and palladium supply and demand are expressed in terms of fine metal content.  All references in this publication to “ounces” refer to troy ounces. 

**One troy ounce =** 31.103 grammes **One tonne =** 32,151 troy ounces **“dollar”** US dollar unless otherwise stated 

#### Prices: 

Unless otherwise stated, US dollars and their equivalents are for the pm fixes of the London Platinum and Palladium Market. 

Terminology: 

Estimates of **supply** _include_ mine production and the recycling of both scrapped autocatalysts and old jewellery but _exclude_ contributions from above-ground stocks, such as supplies from stocks controlled by state institutions in Russia. 

**Demand** estimates are _net_ of recycling with the exception of autocatalyst and jewellery, where _gross_ demand is shown. i.e. the total amount of metal supplied to these two sectors.  Estimates of recycling from scrapped autocatalysts and jewellery are shown separately as part of supply given their scale and potential for change.  (This year’s survey is the

second in which we have presented jewellery fabrication as gross with a separate series for scrap; prior to this, jewellery was shown on a net basis.)  Estimates of demand exclude the movements of any above-ground stocks held within the specified industries, for example any changes in stocks held by the automotive industry. 

By simple arithmetic, this leaves either a **“Gross Surplus or Deficit”** before any movements in above-ground stocks are considered.  This is a critical measure of the underlying fundamentals of platinum and palladium and indicates the extent to which fabrication demand may have depended on the release of above-ground stocks, or otherwise.  At the same time, this also indicates the change in global above-ground stocks. 

Unless otherwise stated, all references to **“above-ground stocks”** of platinum and palladium refer to stocks of refined metal, of a form and quality accepted as good delivery in the Zurich market and the world’s principal commodity exchanges.  Our supply/demand tables also show **“Estimated Movements in Stocks”** .  These specific movements relate only to above-ground stock holdings for which reasonable estimates of movement can be made and attributed. A listing and breakdown of these appears in the more detailed tables in the Appendices section of this Survey. 

Having allowed for the Estimated Movements in Stocks as defined above, the **“Residual Surplus or Deficit”** is arrived at by deduction.  A **residual deficit** implies the extent to which **_other above-ground stocks_** , including those held by financial institutions and/or investors, were released to meet fabrication demand.  Conversely a **residual surplus** implies the extent to which these **_other above-ground stock_** holdings were added to.  However, this should not be construed as indicating the change in global above-ground stocks.  For this, please refer to the reported Gross Surplus or Deficit. 

**Throughout the tables, totals may not add due to independent rounding.**

## **1. Executive Summary** 

### **1.1 Introduction** 

After a depressed period of trading over the final quarter of 2011, platinum and palladium prices have rallied strongly in the opening weeks of this year.  This improvement has coincided with the re-emergence of concerns over mine production in South Africa (the world’s largest PGM producer), including worries over electricity supplies, the effect of Section 54 safety related stoppages and in particular over recent days, strike action at Impala’s operations.  However, while these supply-side issues have a positive bearing on investor sentiment, it is difficult to ignore the fact that the much larger gold market has experienced similar upward price momentum since the turn of the year, with silver having performed strongly as well. 

Clearly, this resurgence of interest in the precious metals complex as a whole (and gold in particular) is invest

ment driven, with the prime motivations being macro-economic, rather than fundamentally based. These macro factors include the continuing crisis in the eurozone (where multiple sovereign downgrades occurred in January) and importantly, the Federal Reserve Bank’s 25th January announcement that it would continue to target exceptionally low US interest rates for considerably longer than previously expected (until late 2014) – this having also raised expectations of a third round of quantitative easing (QE3). specifically, this runs contrary to its persistently weak underlying fundamentals. Platinum is now characterised by a firmly entrenched record of recurring gross surpluses, with these expected to continue at significant levels over the forecast period. A corollary of this is that above-ground stocks of platinum have grown uncomfortably large over recent years (equivalent to eight months’ fabrication demand at the end of 2011) and are expected to rise still further while these surplus conditions prevail. Meanwhile, although palladium’s underlying fundamentals may have been similarly sidelined of late, they are significantly more supportive. Firstly (and in contrast to platinum), palladium has registered an extended period of underlying gross deficits over the last ten years or so, with these being forecast to continue through to 2014. Secondly, sales of excess palladium stocks by the Russian government (which have long over-shadowed the palladium market) are expected to reduce from this year and conclude in 2013. However, while these factors are positive for palladium, it must also be acknowledged that aboveground palladium stocks (although eroding) remain substantial – we estimate the equivalent of almost fifteen months’ fabrication demand as at end-2011. ### **1.2 Platinum** Looking at the prospects for prices over the forecast period, notwithstanding the current situation in Sout

h Africa (RSA), it is difficult to imagine conditions there of sufficient severity to materially reduce the 0.9M ounce gross surplus of platinum we project for 2012 – a projection which already includes reduced expectations for RSA mine production (relative to our previous forecast), against which we in any case factor in a contingency. Furthermore, while the strike action at Impala is understood to adversely impact platinum production by 3,000 ounces per day, this could be readily offset by the combined impact of reduced jewellery fabrication (mainly in China) and increased scrap flow – both of which are quite possible given platinum’s recent price escalation. Meanwhile, the prospects for platinum demand this year in the vitally important autocatalyst sector (more than 40% of overall fabrication demand) remain weak and are expected to improve only moderately over the forecast period. In the main, this is due to platinum’s reliance on diesel applications (already heavily damaged by substitution in favour of palladium), the majority of which is concentrated in Europe where diesel’s share of production is especially large. As a result, around half of global autocatalyst platinum demand is exposed to the double-dip recession Europe now faces, amid huge uncertainties over the continuing eurozone sovereign debt crisis. We are therefore of the view that platinum’s recent rally will not be sustained beyond a resolution of the strike at Impala (where the re-hiring of sacked workers is underway as we write). With the likelihood of significant volatility over the remainder of this year, including frequent bouts of renewed price weakness, we forecast an average price for platinum in 2012 of $1,620. Thereafter, as Europe emerges from recession and with the macro environment for precious metals investment still intact (supported by continuing low US interest rates and the likelihood of QE3) we believe there is scope for investor driven price appreciation in 2013, despite little improvement in platinum’s underlying fundamentals. Accordingly, we forecast an average price for platinum in 2013 of $1,690. However, as we move into 2014, we believe the impending conclusion of the Fed’s “low for longer” interest rate policy will have negative consequences for gold and precious metals prices in general. With platinum remaining in gross surplus at that time (although somewhat reduced), but with above-ground stocks having escalated still further, we believe platinum will weaken as the investment climate deteriorates ahead of an anticipated change in US interest rate policy. The key driver of this is autocatalyst demand. Having recovered strongly from the recession of 2009 (unlike platinum), autocatalyst demand for palladium is expected to reach a record high in 2012, with this uptrend continuing with further highs through to 2014. While the situation in Europe poses some risk for autocatalyst palladium demand, it is more broadly based geographically (relative to platinum) with significant exposure to improving automotive production in North America and a number of growing vehicle markets including China. Furthermore, palladium is strongly dominant in gasoline applications which represent three-quarters of global vehicle production. Together with broad stability in its other applications (although declines are forecast in jewellery and dental), we expect this to generate sufficient overall demand growth to offset forecast increases in palladium supply; these being driven largely by strong gains in autocatalyst recycling. Therefore, while palladium’s recent gains may not have been directly driven by its fundamentals, we believe its foundations are sufficiently solid to justify this price appreciation. Therefore, we forecast an average price for palladium in 2012 of $735 (a record high), with further gains next year lifting the 2013 average to $785. Thereafter, while the investment climate for precious metals is expected to weaken during 2014 (with gold, silver and platinum prices expected to ease in annual average terms), we believe palladium’s superior fundamentals will enable it to outperform its peers. We forecast an average price for palladium of $935 in 2014. In conjunction with our forecast platinum prices, a closer convergence of platinum and palladium prices is implicit in these projections, especially so for 2014. With the differential having remained close to the $1,000 level (in favour of platinum) over the five years to 2011, we expect this to erode somewhat over the next two years, before narrowing sharply to a forecast $630 in 2014. In view of their comparative fundamentals, this seems to us a reasonable conclusion – especially so when one consi

Economic Assumptions** ### **2.1 Introduction** Thomson Reuters GFMS’ views for the forecast period are presented in the form of three probability-weighted scenarios, namely the Base Case Scenario, Scenario B and Scenario C. Under our **Base Case** , we expect to see a slowdown in world GDP growth this year. This will mainly be driven by the ongoing sovereign debt crisis in Europe, fiscal policy tightening in places and a reduction in industrial production in major advanced economies. Although developing world countries continue to expand, their growth is likely to moderate due to tight monetary conditions in a number of countries and downward pressure on external demand stemming from economic and financial problems in industrialised countries. Nevertheless, we expect the world economy to improve gradually over the final two years of our forecast. We view this as the most likely scenario with a 45% probability. Under our more bullish **Scenario B** , to which we assign a 40% probability, we expect global economic recovery with higher growth rates in both the major advanced and developing countries over the forecast period. We assume that the US government and the Federal Reserve will continue to implement ultraloose monetary and fiscal policies, at least until late-2014. We therefore expect to see the dollar weakening and inflation rising during this period, with the latter reaching an annual average of 5.8% in 2014. Furthermore, we assume that under this scenario the European Central Bank (ECB) will take more aggressive measures in order to tackle the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis. Under our bearish **Scenario C** , with a 15% probability, we assume that no further easing measures would take place in the United States, combined with a faster pace of fiscal consolidation in Europe. As a result, world GDP growth is forecast to slow considerably this year and to remain sluggish over the remainder of the forecast period, particularly in the developed world. Under this scenario, therefore, we expect very low levels of inflation together with a stronger US dollar. The sections below start by describing the background to the current economic situation. We then discuss in more detail each of the three economic scenarios, with a particular focus on some key individual countries. ### **2.2 Economic Backdrop** The strains of the European sovereign debt crisis (which is far from being resolved), rising unemployment and ongoing austerity measures, raises the prospect of a recession here in the early part of this year.

Furthermore, the recent downgrade by Standard & Poor’s of the European bail-out fund (European Financial Stability Fund; EFSF), following its mass downgrade of nine Eurozone countries, including France and Austria, raises pressure on the Eurozone. It is believed that the downgrade may affect the ability of the EFSF to raise long-term funds and therefore its ability to contain the region’s debt crisis. Meanwhile, yield spreads between German bonds and those of stressed countries remain unsustainably wide. For example, Portugal’s bond yields rose sharply after its debt rating was cut to ‘junk’ status, while costs of borrowing for both Spain and Italy remain worryingly high. As the sovereign debt crisis continues to intensify, the most pronounced risk is of a break-up of the common currency area, with Greece being the obvious candidate to assume this role. Although the Greek government introduced severe austerity measures in both 2011 and 2012, it failed to meet its targets and the country’s debt burden has continued to rise. According to European Commission estimates, Greece’s debt will near 200% of GDP this year. The situation has become more acute as Greece and its private creditors have struggled to reach an agreement on loan write-offs. Without a deal, Greece would not receive the next tranche of bailout funds required to pay its debts; the country faces a debt repayment of €14.5 billion in March this year. In the meantime, while the ECB refrains from direct quantitative easing, the European debt crisis continues to escalate, intensifying worries over its impact on the world economy. Looking across the Atlantic, US

GDP growth, the world’s largest economy, slowed significantly last year, particularly in the first half.  The US’ deteriorating fiscal position (aggravated by a lack of a concrete mediumterm debt reduction plan), higher volatility in the financial markets, a weak housing market and elevated levels of unemployment put a major drag on US economic growth.  Although there have recently been positive economic signs, downside risks to US GDP growth this year remain strong.  Furthermore, there is still a lack of progress in addressing the country’s debt problem, which raises doubts regarding the strength of the US economy. 

### **2.3 Base Case Scenario** 

Real global **GDP growth** is expected to fall to an annual average of 2.3% this year due to a further deterioration in the Eurozone debt crisis and its impact on developed and developing countries’ growth rates.  Looking ahead, we expect to see a gradual improvement in the world economy over the following two years, with expansionary monetary policies remaining in place in key countries and the possible implementation of other global reflationary measures during this period.  As a result, the world economy is forecast to grow at annual average rates of 3.0% and 3.5% in 2013 and 2014 respectively. 

According to preliminary government estimates, GDP growth in the **United States** reached 2.8% in the final three months of 2011 (on an annualised basis), up from a 1.8% growth rate during the previous 

quarter.  The economy grew at its fastest rate in more than a year and a half, which was largely driven by robust stock accumulation by businesses and stronger consumer spending.  However, although there has been a clear reduction in recession risk in the United States, the economic recovery there remains fragile due to risks stemming from the ongoing Eurozone sovereign debt crisis and a slowdown in the global economy.  Furthermore, the housing market remains depressed and, although the labour market saw some improvements towards the end of the year, the unemployment rate remains elevated.  We therefore expect US GDP growth to slow to 1.5% this year before economic conditions improve in the final two years of the forecast.  Even so, subsequent US growth is predicted to be relatively subdued due to the excessive level of federal debt, with an annual average rise of 2.0% and 2.2% in 2013 and 2014 respectively. 

Economic activity in **Europe** weakened further in the third quarter of 2011 to an annualised rate of 1.4%. This was largely driven by the escalating sovereign debt crisis and a slowdown in economic growth in Germany and France, the two largest economies in the Eurozone. European countries continue to face considerable challenges this year.  In particular, debt crisis is expected to deepen further in 2012 following the failure of the EU summit in December 2011 to provide a definitive solution.  As a result, funding pressures will persist in spite of the ECB’s efforts to enhance liquidity.

### **2.5 Scenario C** 

Under our bearish **Scenario C** , we expect to see sluggish economic performance, particularly in the developed world, with growth rates remaining at historically low levels throughout the forecast period, especially for a post-recession phase of economic growth.  World GDP growth is therefore forecast to average around 2.3% per annum between 2012 and 2014. 

GDP growth in the world’s largest economy, the **United States** , is expected to slow this year to an annual average of 1.0%.  Central to this poor performance is

In addition, elevated levels of unemployment, coupled with a weak housing market, will put further pressure on the US economy. of southern European countries, which in turn will continue to reduce the region’s growth. Looking ahead, amid faster fiscal policy tightening, we expect economic growth in Europe to remain weak for the remainder of the forecast, registering an annual average of 1.0% and 0.9% in 2013 and 2014 respectively.

Real GDP growth is therefore expected to be relatively subdued over the forecast period, registering an average of 1.0% per annum between 2012 and 2014. 

Against this backdrop, developing countries are expected to substantially outperform the industrialised world (in terms of their economic growth), partly as a consequence of their generally healthier fiscal positions. Nevertheless, weak export markets will ensure that even developing markets will grow at a slower pace than under the Base Case.  Although **Chinese** growth will most likely be the strongest among the larger countries in this group, it will still average a relatively modest 7.5% per annum between 2012 and 2014. However, while opportunities remain for palladium to increase its penetration of individual applications, those gains will be considerably less within the horizon of this forecast than those enjoyed over recent years.  For example, in the light duty diesel sector, the introduction of bi-metallic platinum/palladium catalysts (where platinum remains

### **7.1 Introduction** 

Since the mid-2000s, investment demand for both platinum and palladium has risen strongly, with the temporary exception of the massive sell-off that impacted the whole of the commodities complex during late 2008.  In essence, the growth in investment demand has been the most important driver of the increase in platinum and palladium prices in recent years.  Behind this surge in investment have been several factors.  First, thee has been a general rise in investor interest in precious metals, particularly gold, with both platinum and palladium also benefiting from this trend.  Second, support has come from the broad growth in investment demand for commodities as an asset class, boosted by a weakening US dollar against most currencies in recent years. 

Finally, both metals’ supply/demand fundamentals at times have had a positive impact on investor sentiment. For example, supply concerns related to South African mine production not only triggered a sharp rise in speculative inflows into the platinum market in early 2008 but also provided support during periods of price weakness.  In the case of palladium, the belief in its convergence with the platinum price, as a result of the metal’s ongoing substitution gains in autocatalyst fabrication, has also frequently generated interest, as have expectations of a near term cessation of Russian government stock sales.
